step.detail:
Question: What does this official page say about raising concerns/complaints, time limits, and redress or compensation for NHS care in Wales? Quote the key wording.
The page says to raise concerns “as soon as possible,” first by talking to the staff involved; if that does not help, you can contact the health board or trust’s complaints team. It says “You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint,” though it is best to do so as soon as possible, and if it is longer than 12 months the team may still deal with it if there are good reasons for the delay. For redress/compensation, this page does not mention compensation or redress; it only says that concerns raised after 31 March 2026 should follow the new process via “Listening to people: NHS Wales complaints, incidents and redress process.”
✓ quote found in the page: "If you have concerns about your care or treatment, talk to the staff involved with your care as soon as possible."

step.detail:
Question: What does this official page say about claims and redress governance for NHS Wales? Quote the key wording that explains the compensation route.
The page says claims for compensation arise from a complaint or patient-safety incident, and that NHS Wales has introduced redress as a process where NHS organisations must investigate to decide whether there is qualifying liability and a right to compensation. The Welsh Risk Pool administers the risk pooling arrangement and handles reimbursement once claims are settled.
✓ quote found in the page: "Claims for compensation are made once a concern resulting from a complaint, or an incident occurs concerning patient safety."
✓ quote found in the page: "In addition to this, NHS Wales has introduced the concept of redress, where there is an obligation of NHS organisations to investigate complaints or concerns to assess if there is qualifying liability and therefore the right for compensation."
✓ quote found in the page: "The Welsh Risk Pool service has been delegated responsibility to administer the risk pooling arrangement for NHS Wales and this includes the management of reimbursement to member organisations once claims have been settled."

Question: What does this official page say about time limits and when the Ombudsman can consider a complaint? Quote the key wording.
The page says the Ombudsman will check whether you complained within a year of knowing about the issue, and it will also consider whether you already complained to the organisation and gave it enough time to respond. It says they think 12 weeks is a reasonable time for a final reply, though health and social care cases may take longer. The page also says most complaints are responded to within 6-9 weeks, but if more in-depth assessment is needed it may take at least 12 weeks for allocation to an officer.

route.summary: University Hospital of Wales is run by Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, so your first step is the NHS Wales 'Listening to People' complaint route with the Health Board. If their answer is not enough, you can usually go to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales after giving the Health Board a chance to reply; compensation in Wales can also be considered through the NHS redress process arising from the complaint, and you can get free help from Llais plus your records from the Health Records Department.

steps.body: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
steps.what: University Hospital of Wales is part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board in NHS Wales, so this is a public NHS Wales complaint. The Health Board says to raise concerns with the staff involved first; if that does not resolve it, use its 'Listening to People' complaints process by phone, email, post, or its downloadable complaints form. The newer Welsh Government page says concerns raised after 31 March 2026 follow 'Listening to People', while older pages still refer to 'Putting Things Right'.
steps.deadline: "You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint. However, it is best to talk to someone as soon as possible."
missing: Whether the patient has already complained to the Health Board

steps.what: If the Health Board's complaint answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. Its official pages say it is very unlikely to help unless you complained to the organisation first and gave it time to reply; its fact sheet says 12 weeks is a reasonable time for a final reply and complaints should usually reach the Ombudsman within a year of knowing about the issue.
steps.deadline: "you complained to us within a year of knowing about the issue"
requires: Complaint to Cardiff and Vale University Health Board first

steps.what: For harm from NHS care in Wales, compensation can arise through the NHS Wales complaints/redress process rather than only by a separate court claim. Official NHS Wales Shared Services pages say claims for compensation are made once a concern from a complaint or patient-safety incident occurs, and NHS organisations must investigate to assess whether there is qualifying liability and therefore a right to compensation.
requires: A concern/complaint or patient-safety incident about NHS care
steps.appliesIf: Public NHS Wales care.

sources.quote: Claims for compensation are made once a concern resulting from a complaint, or an incident occurs concerning patient safety.

NHS Wales has introduced the concept of redress, where there is an obligation of NHS organisations to investigate complaints or concerns to assess if there is qualifying liability and therefore the right for compensation.

says.detail:
NHS Wales complaints and concerns: Putting Things Right | GOV.WALES (https://www.gov.wales/nhs-wales-complaints-and-concerns-putting-things-right)
The page says to raise concerns “as soon as possible,” first by talking to the staff involved; if that does not help, you can contact the health board or trust’s complaints team. It says “You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint,” though it is best to do so as soon as possible, and if it is longer than 12 months the team may still deal with it if there are good reasons for the delay. For redress/compensation, this page does not mention compensation or redress; it only says that concerns raised after 31 March 2026 should follow the new process via “Listening to people: NHS Wales complaints, incidents and redress process.”
Quotes: "If you have concerns about your care or treatment, talk to the staff involved with your care as soon as possible." | "If this does not help, or you do not want to speak to the staff, you can contact the health board or trust‘s complaints team." | "You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint. However, it is best to talk to someone as soon as possible." | "Concerns raised after 31 March 2026 should follow the new process via Listening to people: NHS Wales complaints, incidents and redress process"

Complaints - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board (https://cavuhb.nhs.wales/our-services/cardiff-and-vale-apb/complaints/)
The page says that if you are unhappy, you should raise concerns through the relevant complaints process, and for APB Support Team issues you should first try talking to the staff member concerned; if that does not resolve it, use the Health Board’s “Putting Things Right” complaints process. Claims and Redress Governance - NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership (https://nwssp.nhs.wales/ourservices/welsh-risk-pool/about-the-welsh-risk-pool-service/claims-and-redress-governance/)
The page says claims for compensation arise from a complaint or patient-safety incident, and that NHS Wales has introduced redress as a process where NHS organisations must investigate to decide whether there is qualifying liability and a right to compensation. The Welsh Risk Pool administers the risk pooling arrangement and handles reimbursement once claims are settled.
Quotes: "Claims for compensation are made once a concern resulting from a complaint, or an incident occurs concerning patient safety." | "In addition to this, NHS Wales has introduced the concept of redress, where there is an obligation of NHS organisations to investigate complaints or concerns to assess if there is qualifying liability and therefore the right for compensation." | "The Welsh Risk Pool service has been delegated responsibility to administer the risk pooling arrangement for NHS Wales and this includes the management of reimbursement to member organisations once claims have been settled."

Complain: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board. University Hospital of Wales is part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board in NHS Wales, so this is a public NHS Wales complaint. The Health Board says to raise concerns with the staff involved first; if that does not resolve it, use its 'Listening to People' complaints process by phone, email, post, or its downloadable complaints form. The newer Welsh Government page says concerns raised after 31 March 2026 follow 'Listening to People', while older pages still refer to 'Putting Things Right'.

If that fails: Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. If the Health Board's complaint answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. Its official pages say it is very unlikely to help unless you complained to the organisation first and gave it time to reply; its fact sheet says 12 weeks is a reasonable time for a final reply and complaints should usually reach the Ombudsman within a year of knowing about the issue. (one official source)

Compensation: NHS Wales. For harm from NHS care in Wales, compensation can arise through the NHS Wales complaints/redress process rather than only by a separate court claim. Official NHS Wales Shared Services pages say claims for compensation are made once a concern from a complaint or patient-safety incident occurs, and NHS organisations must investigate to assess whether there is qualifying liability and therefore a right to compensation. (one official source)

Finding a lawyer: The Law Society. To find a solicitor for a clinical negligence case in Wales, use the Law Society's official 'Find a Solicitor' service for England and Wales. Its page says you can filter by legal issue and by postcode, town or country, which lets a patient search for clinical negligence solicitors near Cardiff or elsewhere in Wales. (one official source)

Paying for help: Ministry of Justice. An official Ministry of Justice page lets a patient search for legal aid advisers for clinical negligence in England and Wales. The page found is an adviser finder rather than a full public eligibility checker, and it says the adviser will ask about the problem and finances to work out if legal aid is available. (one official source)

Free help: Llais. Llais is the free independent body in Wales that helps people have a voice in health and social care and has pages for making a complaint or raising a concern. For this patient's area, the local service is Llais Cardiff & The Vale. (one official source)

Your records: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board. To get a copy of your own medical records from Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, the official pages say to contact or write to the Health Records Department. The site gives a dedicated records email and phone number, and points to the Health Board's access-to-health-records information rather than an online request form. (one official source)

Clinical guidance: Welsh Government / NICE. The official Welsh Government page says all NICE guidelines and quality standards are available to use in Wales, though most are not mandatory. That makes NICE the main published national clinical guidance body relevant to emergency care here, subject to Welsh legislation. (one official source)

Question: What does this official page say about claims and redress governance for NHS Wales? Quote the key wording that explains the compensation route.
The page says claims for compensation arise from a complaint or patient-safety incident, and that NHS Wales has introduced redress as a process where NHS organisations must investigate to decide whether there is qualifying liability and a right to compensation. The Welsh Risk Pool administers the risk pooling arrangement and handles reimbursement once claims are settled.
